spec.title: Namib
spec.subtitle: A coast of stone and fog, ancient and austere

chapters.label: CHAPTER 01 · BOUNDLESS HORIZON
chapters.heading: The Atlantic wind sweeps the dunes into endless waves.
chapters.body: The Namib runs more than 2,000 kilometres along the Atlantic, from Angola through Namibia to South Africa. Its northern stretch, called the Moçâmedes Desert, extends 450 kilometres from the Angola-Namibia border. Inland the land rises to the Great Escarpment, reaching up to 200 kilometres from the sea. The desert holds some of the world's driest regions, rivaled only by the Atacama.

chapters.label: CHAPTER 02 · SILENT FOG
chapters.heading: Morning fog rolls inland, a veil of ocean breath.
chapters.subheading: Moisture arrives on a cold current.
chapters.body: Fog forms when the cold Benguela Current meets warm air from the Hadley cell, creating a belt that frequently envelops the coast. More than 180 days of thick fog occur each year, providing vital moisture for desert life. The fog has wrecked ships along the Skeleton Coast, leaving over a thousand wrecks scattered across the sands.

heroImage.attribution: Giles Laurent · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

chapters.label: CHAPTER 03 · LIVING STONE
chapters.heading: Life clings to rock and sand, defying age.
chapters.body: The Namib may be the oldest desert, enduring arid conditions for roughly 55-80 million years. It supports endemic species, from arthropods to mountain zebras. Along the coast, brown fur seals and shorebirds thrive, feeding the Skeleton Coast's lions. Inland, dunes rise up to 300 metres, forming a sea of pink and orange sand.
